newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan gives cool response to China vaccine offer.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan gives cool response to China vaccine offer.

text.p: China on Monday offered to supply Taiwan with a vaccine for hog foot and mouth disease, but local farm officials said quality and political obstacles meant a deal was unlikely.

"Taiwan only imports vaccines from makers with high international quality standards," Sung Hwa-tsung, a senior official of the cabinet's Council of Agriculture, told Reuters when asked whether Taiwan could accept mainland vaccines.
Taiwan has begun emergency imports of vaccines to inoculate its healthy livestock against hog foot and mouth disease, which has been detected at more than 1,000 of the island's 25,000 feedlots.
Millions of doses were being airlifted from Britain, France, the United States and other sources whose production met Taiwan's quality requirements, Sung said.
Without passing judgment on China's vaccines, Sung expressed concern that poor-quality vaccines could exacerbate problems rather than solve them.
"An unsafe vaccine could be worse than the disease itself," Sung said without further explanation.
Taiwan still remembers a major case of vaccine contamination in 1996 in which thousands of hepatitis C vaccines imported from Italy were found to be contaminated with hepatitis B.
Sung added that Nationalist-ruled Taiwan had no authority to import vaccines from communist China, the island's political arch-rival since a civil war split them in 1949.
"Taiwan's Board of Foreign Trade has not issued permission to import animal vaccines made on the mainland," Sung said.
China made the vaccine offer through its semi-official Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Strait.
"We received a letter from the mainland expressing its intention to provide pig vaccines," said an official at the Straits Exchange Foundation, the local counterpart to China's association.
The official declined to comment on the letter in detail.
As of late on Friday, the virus had been detected on 1,008 hog farms, although only 160,315 pigs were reported to have been slaughtered, according to official statistics.

A mass slaughter of all hogs -- healthy or otherwise -- was under way on farms struck by the deadly contagion, with experts reporting that more than 886,000 pigs would have to be destroyed, the agriculture council said.
Industry sources quoted by the ruling Nationalist Party on Wednesday estimated that about 15 percent of Taiwan's 11 million swine -- or 1.6 million animals -- would be affected directly.
The agriculture council banned all pork exports after confirming the outbreak on March 20, when the virus was found in just nine feedlots.
